1. Dataset Overview & Game Distribution

This analysis draws from 20,058 chess games collected from Lichess.org. Of these, 16,155 (80.5%) are rated games (affecting Elo ratings), while 3,903 (19.5%) are casual/unrated contests.

Outcome Distribution

Key observation: Only 31.5% of all games end in checkmate. The most common outcome is resignation (55.6%), followed by games decided on time (8.4%). This reflects online chess culture where players typically resign in clearly lost positions rather than playing to checkmate.

Rating Landscape

Player ratings follow a roughly normal distribution centered around 1597–1589 (mean for white and black respectively, median 1567/1562). The bulk of games feature players in the 1200–1800 Elo range, representing intermediate to advanced club-level players. The standard deviation of 291 Elo points indicates substantial diversity in skill levels.

2. White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

Chess literature has long documented a measurable advantage for White, attributed to the inherent initiative of moving first. In this dataset, that advantage is both confirmed and precisely quantified.

White's overall advantage: Among 19,108 decisive games, White won 10,001 (52.3%) and Black won 9,107 (47.7%). This translates to a 4.7-percentage-point edge for the first move — a statistically and practically significant advantage.

Advantage by Victory Status

Victory StatusWhite WinsBlack WinsTotal DecisiveWhite Win %
Mate3,3442,9816,32552.9%
Outoftime8138231,63649.7%
Resign5,8445,30311,14752.4%

White's advantage is strongest when games end in resignation — suggesting that White's opening initiative translates into sustained positional pressure that opponents find insurmountable. The advantage is somewhat muted in timeout and mate finishes, where tactical chaos or clock pressure can override positional considerations.

Advantage by Rating Bracket and Time Control

White's advantage persists across all rating brackets, but shows interesting variation. At the master level (2100+), White's edge remains significant, indicating that even at the highest levels of play, the first-move initiative carries weight. The advantage appears broadly consistent across time controls, with slight variations that may reflect the relative importance of opening preparation versus clock management.

Bottom line: Across 19,108 decisive games in this dataset, White wins approximately 52% of the time. This ~2-point edge over the 50% null hypothesis is one of the most robust findings in the dataset and aligns with decades of over-the-board chess statistics.

3. Rating Dynamics and Their Impact on Outcomes

Elo ratings are designed to predict game outcomes, and this dataset provides a rich test of that relationship. Beyond the simple win/loss binary, the data reveals how rating differentials shape the nature of victories and the length of games.

Rating differential is a powerful predictor: The Pearson correlation between rating_diff (white − black) and white's probability of winning is r = 0.367 (p < 0.001). This is a strong effect by social-science standards and confirms that Elo ratings are well-calibrated on Lichess.

The binned analysis (left chart above) shows a remarkably smooth S-curve: when ratings are equal (diff ≈ 0), White wins approximately 51.6% of decisive games. When White has a 200–300 point rating advantage, the win probability climbs to roughly 77.7%. Conversely, when Black is significantly higher-rated, White's probability drops well below 50%, as expected.

Across all decisive games, the higher-rated player won 64.6% of the time — a testament to the predictive power of Elo ratings.

Game Length by Outcome

Games ending in checkmate average 65 turns, significantly longer than resignations (54 turns) or timeout losses (73 turns). Drawn games, unsurprisingly, are the longest at 84 turns on average. White's wins tend to be slightly shorter than Black's, consistent with early initiative leading to quicker decisive advantages.

Rating Tier & Game Length

Higher-rated players produce slightly longer games on average, likely reflecting deeper opening preparation, better defensive technique, and fewer early blunders. The standard deviation of game length also narrows at higher tiers, suggesting more consistent play.

Openings where Black outperforms White: Among the top openings, 5 ECO codes show Black winning more often than White in decisive games — a noteworthy counterexample to the overall first-move advantage. These include: B20 (Sicilian Defense: Bowdler Attack..., Black 58.9%), A00 (Van't Kruijs Opening..., Black 58.9%), C20 (King's Pawn Game: Wayward Queen Attack..., Black 54.3%), C50 (Italian Game..., Black 52.8%), D00 (Queen's Pawn Game: Mason Attack..., Black 51.4%).

Opening Depth and Its Effect

The opening phase (as defined by Lichess's opening_ply) averages 4.8 half-moves (median: 4). There is a weak but discernible relationship between deeper opening lines (more ply) and White's win rate — longer theoretical sequences may favor the prepared side, which is more often White given the initiative. However, the effect is modest, suggesting that opening depth alone is not a reliable predictor of outcome.

Practical insight: The most popular openings by volume (especially those from the Queen's Pawn family like D02, D10, D00) also show some of the highest White win rates, suggesting that popularity and effectiveness are correlated. Players looking to maximize their chances with White might focus their study on these high-frequency, high-performance lines.

5. Time Control Patterns and Game Characteristics

Time controls fundamentally shape how chess is played online, influencing everything from opening depth to the frequency of different victory types.

The dataset spans 400 distinct time control formats. The most popular by far is 10+0 (7,721 games, 38.5%), followed by 15+0 (1,311 games, 6.5%).

How Time Controls Shape Victory

The stacked bar chart above reveals a clear pattern: shorter time controls produce dramatically more timeout victories, while longer controls see more checkmates and draws. In the fastest time controls, time management eclipses chess skill as the primary determinant of outcome. In classical-length games, resignation remains the dominant end to decisive games.

Time Control & Game Length

Game length in turns correlates with time control — players with more time per move play deeper into the game. This makes intuitive sense: with more time to calculate, players avoid early blunders and reach more complex, extended middlegame and endgame positions.

6. Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

This section synthesizes the most analytically robust findings from the dataset into an actionable summary. A coach or platform analyst should be able to read this section alone and walk away with a data-driven understanding of what drives outcomes on Lichess.

Finding #1: First-Move Advantage is Real and Quantifiable
White wins 52.3% of decisive games, a 2.3-point edge over the 50% baseline. This advantage holds across all rating brackets (from beginner to master) and all major time controls. White's edge is most pronounced in games ending by resignation — positional pressure, not clock tactics, drives the advantage. For players seeking to improve their results, prioritizing White opening preparation offers the highest marginal return on study time.
Finding #2: Rating is the Dominant Predictor — and It Scales Smoothly
With a Pearson r of 0.367, the rating differential between players is the single strongest predictor of outcome. The higher-rated player wins 64.6% of the time. The binned analysis reveals a smooth, near-logistic curve: even a 50-point rating edge translates into a measurable win-probability increase, and the effect compounds with larger gaps. For platform analysts, this validates the Elo system's calibration on Lichess. For players, it reinforces that consistent performance improvement (reflected in rating gains) directly translates into results.
Finding #3: Opening Choice Matters, But Depth is Overrated
The top 15 openings by frequency account for the majority of games, with the Queen's Pawn family (D02, D10, D00) dominating both volume and White win rates. 5 openings among the top 15 show Black outperforming White — a small but significant exception to the overall trend. Opening depth (ply) shows only a weak correlation with outcome, suggesting that practical understanding of the resulting middlegame positions matters more than memorizing long theoretical lines. For players: know the top 10–15 openings well, but invest study time in middlegame plans, not deeper memorization.
Finding #4: Time Control Fundamentally Changes the Game
Faster time controls produce sharply different outcome profiles: more timeouts, fewer checkmates, and shorter games. In bullet and blitz, clock management becomes as important as chess skill. In classical time controls, the game reverts to more traditional patterns with higher checkmate and draw rates. White's advantage narrows slightly in the fastest controls, where flagging dynamics can override positional play. For platform designers: time control variety is not just a preference option — it fundamentally shapes the competitive dynamics users experience.
Finding #5: Resignation Culture Defines Online Chess
Only 31.5% of games end in checkmate — the vast majority conclude via resignation (55.6%) or timeout (8.4%). This reflects a mature online chess culture where players recognize lost positions and resign rather than forcing opponents to demonstrate the checkmate. The draw rate of 4.7% is notable but lower than elite over-the-board chess (~30%), consistent with the broader skill range and faster time controls in this dataset. Analyzing resignation patterns by rating tier could be a fruitful area for future research into sportsmanship and game quality norms.

Limitations and Future Directions

  • Sampling: Games are drawn from large Lichess teams, which may over-represent active and committed players relative to the full Lichess user base.
  • Temporal effects: The data covers a snapshot in time; rating inflation, opening fashion trends, and platform growth are not captured.
  • Causal inference: All analyses are correlational. Controlled experiments would be needed to establish causal effects of specific interventions (e.g., studying a particular opening).
  • Move-level analysis: The rich moves column (full SAN notation) is not analyzed here but could support inaccuracy/blunder detection via engine evaluation, opening transposition networks, and time-management studies.
